How it works

title: UTM Campaign URL Builder

Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What are UTM parameters?
    UTM parameters are tags added to the end of a URL that tell analytics tools where a visit came from. The five standard tags are utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term and utm_content.
  
  
    Which UTM parameters are required?
    Source, medium and campaign are required. Term records a paid search keyword, and content tells apart two links in the same email or advert.
  
  
    What are UTM naming best practices?
    Use lower case throughout, one separator for spaces and a fixed list of mediums such as email, social, and cpc. Consistent names keep each channel in one row of the report.
  
  
    Should I use UTM tags on internal links?
    Leave internal links untagged. UTM tags on links between pages of your own site start a new session and overwrite the visit's original source.

title: SERVQUAL Gap Analysis
text:
Live
SERVQUAL measures service quality as the gap between what customers expect and what they perceive they received. A negative gap means the service fell short of expectations. The five dimensions show where: the physical evidence (tangibles), dependable delivery (reliability), willingness to help (responsiveness), competence and courtesy (assurance), and individual care (empathy).
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. The tool opens on sample hotel figures. Type your own averages, or paste survey responses and let the tool average them.

title: SERVQUAL Gap Analysis
text:
How it works
Each item carries an expectation score E and a perception score P, both on a 1 to 7 scale. The gap for an item is its perception minus its expectation.
Item gap = P − EDimension gap = mean of its item gapsUnweighted SERVQUAL score = mean of the five dimension gapsWeighted SERVQUAL score = Σ (dimension weight ÷ 100) × dimension gap
The weights share 100 points across the five dimensions, so the weighted score reflects what matters most to your customers. The priority dimension is the one with the largest weighted shortfall. The measured gap is the customer gap in the gaps model of service quality. The provider gaps you tag in the Customer Journey Mapper are the causes, and they appear next to the scores when both tools are used on the same device. The dimensions follow Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry (1988), and the item wording is FlairMI’s own.

title: SERVQUAL Gap Analysis
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is SERVQUAL?
    SERVQUAL is a method for measuring service quality, developed by Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry (1988). Customers rate what they expect and what they experienced on 22 items across five dimensions, and the gap between the two measures quality.
  
  
    What are the five SERVQUAL dimensions?
    The five SERVQUAL dimensions are tangibles (facilities and materials), reliability (delivering as promised), responsiveness (quick help), assurance (competence and courtesy that build trust), and empathy (individual attention).
  
  
    How is the SERVQUAL score calculated?
    Each item's gap is perception minus expectation. A dimension's gap is the mean of its items, and the weighted SERVQUAL score multiplies each dimension gap by its importance weight out of 100.
  
  
    What is the gaps model of service quality?
    The gaps model traces the customer gap, between expected and perceived service, to four provider gaps: listening, service design and standards, service performance and communication. SERVQUAL measures the customer gap.
  
  
    Is this SERVQUAL Gap Analysis tool free?
    Yes. The SERVQUAL Gap Analysis tool is free and opens straight away in any modern browser, including on a phone. Scores and pasted responses are processed in your browser and stay on your device.

title: Robots.txt and Sitemap Generator
text:
In progress
The robots.txt file tells crawlers which parts of a site to skip. The sitemap lists the pages you want found. Together they steer how search engines and AI systems read a site. Since 2023, AI companies publish separate crawler names for model training and for search answers, so a site can allow one and block the other.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Set the paths to keep out of search, choose which AI crawlers to block, list the site’s URLs and download both files.

title: Robots.txt and Sitemap Generator
text:
How it works
The robots.txt starts with a rule for all crawlers, adds a block rule for each AI crawler you tick, and ends with the sitemap location.
User-agent: *Disallow: /admin/User-agent: GPTBotDisallow: /Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
The sitemap follows the sitemaps.org protocol: one host, at most 50,000 URLs per file, with an optional last-modified date per URL. Robots.txt is a request that reputable crawlers honour. Private pages need a login to stay private.

title: Robots.txt and Sitemap Generator
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is a robots.txt file?
    A robots.txt file is a text file at the root of a website that tells crawlers which paths they may fetch. Reputable crawlers honour it. Private pages need a login to stay private.
  
  
    How do I block AI crawlers in robots.txt?
    Add a user-agent group for each AI crawler with Disallow: /. Training crawlers include GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot and Google-Extended. Answer crawlers include OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot and blocking them removes the site from AI search answers.
  
  
    What is an XML sitemap?
    An XML sitemap is a file that lists the URLs you want search engines to find, with optional last-modified dates. It follows the sitemaps.org protocol, holds up to 50,000 URLs per file, and is referenced from robots.txt.
  
  
    Does robots.txt remove a page from Google?
    Only partly. A page blocked in robots.txt can still appear if other sites link to it. Use a noindex tag to keep a page out of search results.
  
  
    Is this Robots.txt and Sitemap Generator free?
    Yes. The Robots.txt and Sitemap Generator is free and opens straight away in any modern browser, including on a phone. Everything you enter is processed in your browser and stays on your device.

title: Readability and Headline Analyser
text:
In progress
Readable copy gets read. Short sentences and familiar words let more of the audience understand a message on the first pass, which matters most on a phone. Readability formulas measure two things that predict difficulty: sentence length and word length.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Paste a headline and body copy. The scores and the chart update as you type.

title: Readability and Headline Analyser
text:
How it works
Syllables are estimated from groups of vowels, which is accurate enough for scoring but can miss on unusual words.
Flesch reading ease = 206.835 − 1.015 × (words ÷ sentences) − 84.6 × (syllables ÷ words)Flesch-Kincaid grade = 0.39 × (words ÷ sentences) + 11.8 × (syllables ÷ words) − 15.59
A reading ease of 60 or more reads as plain English. Sentences over 25 words are marked in the text. Passive phrases are flagged by pattern, a form of “to be” followed by a past participle, so check each one by eye.

title: Readability and Headline Analyser
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is the Flesch reading ease score?
    The Flesch reading ease score is a readability formula based on sentence length and syllables per word. Scores run roughly from 0 to 100, higher is easier and 60 to 70 reads as plain English for most adults.
  
  
    How is the Flesch-Kincaid grade level calculated?
    Flesch-Kincaid grade level is 0.39 times the average words per sentence, plus 11.8 times the average syllables per word, minus 15.59. The result approximates the US school grade needed to follow the text.
  
  
    What is a good sentence length for web copy?
    An average of 15 to 20 words per sentence suits most audiences. This tool marks sentences over 25 words, since those are the ones readers most often lose.
  
  
    What makes a good headline for SEO?
    A good SEO headline fits about 600 pixels in search results, puts the target keyword early and makes a specific promise, often with a number. This tool checks each of those.

title: Price Elasticity Calculator
text:
In progress
Price elasticity measures how much demand changes when price changes. It decides whether a price rise increases revenue or loses more in volume than it gains in price.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Enter two prices and the units sold at each. The sample is a hotel member rate raised from 165 to 179.

title: Price Elasticity Calculator
text:
How it works
The arc formula uses the midpoint of the two observations, so the answer is the same whichever price you call the first.
Arc elasticity = [(Q2 − Q1) ÷ ((Q1 + Q2) ÷ 2)] ÷ [(P2 − P1) ÷ ((P1 + P2) ÷ 2)]Elastic when the absolute value is above 1, inelastic below 1Linear demand Q = a − bP through both points: revenue peaks at a ÷ 2b, contribution peaks at (a + b × cost) ÷ 2b
The straight demand line is an assumption that holds best near the two observed prices. Treat the optimal prices as a direction to test.

title: Price Elasticity Calculator
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is price elasticity of demand?
    Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. An elasticity of -1.5 means a 1% price rise cuts sales by about 1.5%.
  
  
    How do you calculate price elasticity with two price points?
    Use the arc formula: the change in quantity over the average quantity, divided by the change in price over the average price. Using the midpoint gives the same answer in either direction.
  
  
    What is the difference between elastic and inelastic demand?
    Demand is elastic when the absolute elasticity is above 1, so a price rise loses more in volume than it gains in price and revenue falls. Demand is inelastic below 1, so a price rise increases revenue.
  
  
    How do you find the profit-maximising price?
    With a straight-line demand curve Q = a minus bP through two observed points, contribution peaks at (a + b times unit cost) divided by 2b. Treat it as a direction to test, since real demand curves bend.

title: Porter’s Five Forces Analyser
text:
In progress
Porter’s Five Forces explains why some industries earn more than others. The stronger the forces, the more of the value created in the industry is taken by buyers, suppliers, rivals, new entrants or substitutes and the less is left as profit.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. It opens on a sample for boutique hotels in Lisbon. Name your own industry and score each statement by how far you agree.

title: Porter’s Five Forces Analyser
text:
How it works
Every statement is written so that agreement means a stronger force. Each force’s score is the mean of its statements on a 1 to 5 scale.
Force score = mean of its statement scoresIndustry attractiveness = 6 − mean of the five force scoresHigh at 3.67 or above, moderate from 2.33, low below 2.33
The radar chart shows the shape of the pressure: a large, even shape means a tough industry, and one long spike points to the force to manage first. Forces scoring 3.5 or more are listed as the main pressures on profit.

title: Porter’s Five Forces Analyser
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What are Porter's Five Forces?
    Porter's Five Forces is a framework for judging how attractive an industry is. The five forces are the threat of new entrants, the bargaining power of suppliers, the bargaining power of buyers, the threat of substitutes and rivalry among existing competitors. Strong forces leave less profit for the firms in the industry.
  
  
    How do you measure the strength of each force?
    Score statements about each force, such as how easily buyers switch provider, from 1 to 5. A force's score is the mean of its statements. This tool rates industry attractiveness as 6 minus the mean of the five force scores.
  
  
    What makes an industry attractive in Porter's Five Forces?
    Weak forces make an industry attractive: high barriers to entry, many small suppliers, buyers who cannot easily switch, few substitutes and calm rivalry. In this tool an attractiveness score of 3.67 or more counts as high.
  
  
    What is an example of Porter's Five Forces for hotels?
    For boutique hotels in Lisbon, buyer power is strong because booking platforms show every rate side by side, and substitutes are strong because short-term rentals compete for the same guests. Supplier power is weak. The tool opens on this example.

title: PESTEL Analysis Builder

Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is a PESTEL analysis?
    A PESTEL analysis is a scan of the six external forces that shape a market: political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal. It picks out changes outside any one firm's control, so a business can plan for them before they arrive.
  
  
    How do you score PESTEL factors?
    Rate each factor's impact on the organisation and its likelihood within the planning period, each from 1 to 5. Multiplying the two gives a priority from 1 to 25 that ranks factors across all six categories.
  
  
    What is the difference between PEST and PESTEL?
    PEST covers political, economic, social and technological factors. PESTEL adds environmental and legal factors, which matter more now that climate rules, sustainability reporting and consumer law shape most markets.
  
  
    What is a PESTEL example for the hotel industry?
    For a European hotel group, tourist tax rises are political, energy costs are economic, demand for wellness breaks is social, AI trip planners are technological, heatwaves are environmental and EU rules on short-term rentals are legal. The tool opens on this example.

title: Net Promoter Score Tracker
text:
In progress
The Net Promoter Score asks one question: how likely is it that you would recommend us to a friend or colleague, from 0 to 10? It is simple to collect and to track. The margin of error is often left out, and a small change between waves can then look like progress when it is noise.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Waves are saved on this device. Enter counts of promoters, passives, and detractors or paste raw scores and add each new wave.

title: Net Promoter Score Tracker
text:
How it works
Promoters score 9 or 10, passives 7 or 8 and detractors 0 to 6.
NPS = % promoters − % detractors, from −100 to +100Standard error = √((pP + pD − (pP − pD)²) ÷ n) × 10095% interval = NPS ± 1.96 × standard error
A change between two waves is flagged as larger than chance when it exceeds the combined margin of error of both waves, a conservative check.

title: Net Promoter Score Tracker
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is Net Promoter Score?
    Net Promoter Score (NPS) is a customer loyalty measure based on one question: how likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague, from 0 to 10? It runs from -100 to +100.
  
  
    How is NPS calculated?
    Subtract the percentage of detractors, who score 0 to 6, from the percentage of promoters, who score 9 or 10. Passives, who score 7 or 8, count in the total only.
  
  
    What is the margin of error for NPS?
    The margin of error for NPS depends on the sample size and the mix of answers. With 400 responses it is often about 7 to 9 points at 95% confidence. This tool calculates it for every survey wave.
  
  
    What is a good NPS score?
    A good NPS varies by industry. Compare with your own previous waves and with competitors measured the same way, since a general benchmark says little about your own market.

    What are meta tags and Open Graph tags?
    Meta tags describe a page to search engines, chiefly the title tag and the meta description. Open Graph tags tell Facebook, LinkedIn and other platforms which title, description and image to show when the page is shared. Twitter card tags do the same for X.
  
  
    How long should a title tag be?
    A title tag should fit about 600 pixels in search results, roughly 50 to 60 characters. Put the most important words first, since longer titles are cut off.
  
  
    How long should a meta description be?
    A meta description should fit about 920 pixels, roughly 150 to 160 characters. Search engines may rewrite it, but a clear summary that matches the page is usually kept.
  
  
    What size should an Open Graph image be?
    An Open Graph image should be 1200 by 630 pixels, a 1.91 to 1 ratio. With one, a shared link shows a large preview card. Most platforms fall back to a small or empty preview when the image is missing.
  
  
    Is this Meta Tag and Open Graph Preview free?
    Yes. The Meta Tag and Open Graph Preview is free and opens straight away in any modern browser, including on a phone. A share image loads from the address you enter, as it would on any web page.

In progress
The GE-McKinsey matrix extends the BCG idea with more than one measure on each axis. Industry attractiveness and competitive strength are each built from four or more weighted factors, so the grid reflects the judgement of the people scoring it, stated openly.

title: GE-McKinsey Matrix
text:
How it works
Each business unit is scored from 1 to 5 on every factor. The weights on each axis share 100 points.
Axis score = Σ (factor weight × factor score) ÷ Σ factor weightsGrid lines at 2.33 and 3.67 split each axis into low, medium and high
The three top-left boxes suggest investing to grow, the diagonal suggests selective investment, and the three bottom-right boxes suggest harvesting or divesting. Competitive strength runs high on the left, as in the original grid.

title: GE-McKinsey Matrix
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is the GE-McKinsey matrix?
    The GE-McKinsey matrix is a nine-box portfolio grid developed by McKinsey for General Electric. It rates each business unit on industry attractiveness and competitive strength, each built from weighted factors, and suggests whether to invest, invest selectively or harvest.
  
  
    How do you calculate GE-McKinsey matrix scores?
    Choose factors for each axis, weight them to total 100 and score each business unit from 1 to 5 on every factor. Each axis score is the weighted mean, and the grid divides each axis at 2.33 and 3.67.
  
  
    What is the difference between the GE-McKinsey and BCG matrices?
    BCG uses one measure per axis, market growth and relative share, and has four boxes. GE-McKinsey builds each axis from four or more weighted factors and has nine boxes, so it suits businesses where growth and share alone mislead.
  
  
    What do the three zones of the GE-McKinsey matrix mean?
    The green zone, top left, means invest and grow. The amber zone, on the diagonal, means invest selectively and manage for earnings. The red zone, bottom right, means harvest or divest.

title: Colour Contrast Checker
text:
In progress
Low contrast makes text hard to read for people with low vision, on a phone in sunlight, or on a cheap screen. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) set minimum contrast ratios, and many public bodies require them.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Pick a text and a background colour. The preview, the ratio, and the pass or fail results update at once.

title: Colour Contrast Checker
text:
How it works
The ratio compares the relative luminance of the lighter colour with the darker one.
Contrast ratio = (Llighter + 0.05) ÷ (Ldarker + 0.05)L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, after converting each sRGB channel to linear lightAA: 4.5 to 1 for normal text, 3 to 1 for large text and interface partsAAA: 7 to 1 for normal text, 4.5 to 1 for large text
Large text means 24 px, or 18.66 px in bold. When a pair fails, the tool suggests the nearest text colour that passes AA, found by changing lightness only.

title: Colour Contrast Checker
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is a good colour contrast ratio?
    WCAG 2 level AA requires a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text and interface parts. Level AAA requires 7 to 1 for normal text.
  
  
    How is the contrast ratio calculated?
    The contrast ratio is (L1 + 0.05) divided by (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the relative luminance of the lighter colour and L2 that of the darker one. Ratios run from 1 to 1 up to 21 to 1.
  
  
    What counts as large text in WCAG?
    Large text in WCAG is 24 pixels or larger, or 18.66 pixels and bold. It needs a lower contrast ratio because it is easier to read.
  
  
    Can brand colours fail contrast checks?
    Yes, brand colours often fail for normal text. A failing brand colour can still be used for large headings, borders or fills with dark or light text on top. The palette check shows which pairings are safe.

One page often has many addresses: with and without www, http and https, with tracking parameters, and with a trailing slash or a bare ending. Search engines may treat each as a separate page and split its ranking signals. A canonical tag names the one preferred address.

title: Canonical Tag Generator
text:
How it works
Each URL passes through the chosen rules in order: protocol, host case, www, fragment, index file, path case, query string and trailing slash.
Tracking parameters removed: utm_*, gclid, gbraid, wbraid, fbclid, msclkid, dclid, mc_cid, mc_eid, _ga, _gl, ref, igshid, yclidRemaining query parameters are sorted, so the same parameters in any order give one URL
The table shows every change made, and the count of distinct canonical URLs shows how many real pages the list holds.

title: Canonical Tag Generator
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is a canonical tag?
    A canonical tag is a link element in a page's head that names the preferred URL for that content. It tells search engines to combine ranking signals from duplicate URLs onto one address.
  
  
    What causes duplicate URLs?
    Duplicate URLs come from tracking parameters, http and https, www and non-www hosts, trailing slashes, index file names and letter case. Each creates another address for the same page.
  
  
    Should canonical URLs have a trailing slash?
    Either form works. Choose one and use it everywhere: in canonical tags, internal links and the sitemap.
  
  
    Should I strip query parameters from canonical URLs?
    Strip parameters that leave the content unchanged, such as UTM tags and click IDs. Keep parameters that select different content, such as a product variant.

title: Brand Equity Assessor
text:
In progress
Keller’s customer-based brand equity model describes brand building as a ladder. Customers must first know the brand (salience), then understand what it offers practically and emotionally (performance and imagery), form views and feelings about it (judgements and feelings), and only then build loyalty and attachment (resonance).
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. It opens on a sample boutique hotel brand. Name your brand and score each statement.

title: Brand Equity Assessor
text:
How it works
Each building block has three statements scored from 1 to 5. A block’s score is the mean of its statements, and the pyramid shades each block by that score.
Block score = mean of its three statementsRational route = mean of performance and judgementsEmotional route = mean of imagery and feelings
The pyramid holds only when each level rests on a stronger one below it. The tool flags any block that outscores the block it depends on, because that higher score has little to hold it up.

title: Brand Equity Assessor
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is Keller's brand equity model?
    Keller's customer-based brand equity (CBBE) model describes brand building as a pyramid of six blocks: salience, performance, imagery, judgements, feelings and resonance. Each level rests on the one below, with resonance, meaning loyalty and attachment, at the top.
  
  
    What are the four steps of the CBBE pyramid?
    The four steps are identity (who are you?), meaning (what are you?), response (what about you?), and relationships (what about you and me?). Salience builds identity, performance and imagery build meaning, judgements and feelings build response and resonance builds the relationship.
  
  
    How do you measure brand equity?
    Ask customers to rate statements for each building block, then compare the blocks. This tool uses three statements per block on a 1 to 5 scale and flags any block that outscores the block it depends on.
  
  
    What are the rational and emotional routes to brand equity?
    The rational route, on the left of the pyramid, is performance and judgements: what the brand does and how customers rate it. The emotional route, on the right, is imagery and feelings: what the brand means and how it makes customers feel.

title: Marketing Attribution Comparison
text:
In progress
Attribution decides which marketing channels get credit for a sale. The choice of model can make the same channel look essential or worthless. Running all five models on the same data shows how much of a channel’s reported performance comes from the data and how much from the model.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Paste conversion paths as channels in order, with conversions and value. The sample is hotel bookings across six channels.

title: Marketing Attribution Comparison
text:
How it works
Each path’s conversions, or its value, are shared across its touches by the model’s weights.
Last click: 100% to the final touchFirst click: 100% to the first touchLinear: equal sharesTime decay: weight 2−k/h, with k touches before the conversion and h the half-lifePosition-based: 40% first, 40% last, 20% shared across the middle
The paths carry no timestamps, so time decay counts touches. The most model-sensitive channel is the one whose share varies most across the five models.

title: Marketing Attribution Comparison
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is marketing attribution?
    Marketing attribution decides how credit for a conversion is shared among the channels a customer touched before buying, such as search, social media and email.
  
  
    What are the common attribution models?
    Last click gives all credit to the final touch and first click to the first. Linear shares it equally, time decay favours touches nearest the conversion, and position-based gives 40% each to the first and last touches and 20% to the middle.
  
  
    Which attribution model should I use?
    The right attribution model depends on the business, so compare them: conclusions that hold under every model are safe, and channels whose credit swings with the model need a test before budgets move.
  
  
    What is the difference between attribution and marketing mix modelling?
    Attribution shares credit among tracked touches on individual paths. Marketing mix modelling estimates channel effects from spend and sales over time, including untracked channels such as television and word of mouth.

title: A/B Test Sample Size and Significance Calculator
text:
In progress
Most A/B tests fail in one of two ways: they stop too early, so a random swing looks like a win, or they run on too little traffic to detect the change that matters. Sizing the test before it starts, and testing the result properly after it ends, prevents both.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Plan a test on the left, or enter a finished test’s results on the right.

title: A/B Test Sample Size and Significance Calculator
text:
How it works
The sample size per variant uses the normal approximation for comparing two proportions.
n = [z1−α/2 √(2 p̄ (1 − p̄)) + z1−β √(p1(1 − p1) + p2(1 − p2))]² ÷ (p2 − p1)²z = (pB − pA) ÷ √(p (1 − p) (1÷nA + 1÷nB)), with p the pooled rate95% interval for the difference = (pB − pA) ± 1.96 √(pA(1 − pA)÷nA + pB(1 − pB)÷nB)
The p-value is two-sided. Decide the sample size before the test starts and read the result once, at the end. Checking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result inflates the false-positive rate.

title: A/B Test Sample Size and Significance Calculator
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    How do you calculate sample size for an A/B test?
    Set the baseline conversion rate, the smallest lift worth detecting, the significance level and the power. This calculator applies the standard two-proportion formula and gives visitors per variant and the run time at your traffic.
  
  
    How do you know if an A/B test is statistically significant?
    An A/B test is statistically significant when a two-proportion z-test gives a p-value below your significance level, usually 0.05. The difference is then unlikely to be chance alone.
  
  
    What is the minimum detectable effect in A/B testing?
    The minimum detectable effect is the smallest lift worth acting on, stated relative to the baseline rate. Halving it roughly quadruples the sample a test needs.
  
  
    Can I stop an A/B test early?
    Run an A/B test to its planned sample size and read the result once, at the end. Checking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives.

title: surveyframe 0.4.0 is on CRAN
text: TL;DR: surveyframe 0.4.0 reached CRAN on 20 August 2026. Install it with install.packages("surveyframe"). This is the largest release so far. It adds multi-criteria decision analysis with 10 methods, a 9-method text-analysis family for open-ended responses, a track of small-sample corrections and a disclosed-amendment and Git-linked provenance trail for .sframe files. It also carries 2 breaking changes, described at the end. Free and open source under the MIT licence.

title: surveyframe 0.4.0 is on CRAN
section: Decision analysis, collected inside the instrument
text:
Decision analysis, collected inside the instrument
Multi-criteria decision analysis usually sits in a gap. Computation packages assume a clean decision matrix already exists. Survey software stops at the questionnaire. Getting from one to the other is manual work, and mistakes enter there.
0.4.0 closes that gap. It ships 10 methods, each carrying a verified literature citation:

The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and the Analytic Network Process (ANP)
The Decision Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory method (DEMATEL)
VIKOR, MOORA, SMART, WASPAS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE and TOPSIS

Two new item types collect the judgement data inside the survey itself. pairwise_comparison uses Saaty’s 1-to-9 ratio scale for AHP and ANP, or a 0-to-4 directed influence scale for DEMATEL. criteria_weight is a constant-sum allocation across criteria. Both render identically in the static HTML survey, the Shiny module and the builder preview.
An aggregation layer turns per-respondent answers into the matrices the methods consume. It validates that every pair was answered, and it combines respondents with the geometric mean for AHP and ANP, which preserves reciprocity, or the arithmetic mean for DEMATEL. AHP judgements are screened for consistency against Saaty’s random-index table, and the consistency-ratio distribution is reported for every study, with or without a filtering threshold declared in advance.
Every ranking method resolves its inputs in the same order, and records where each number came from, so a results table can state the provenance of what it shows. sensitivity_analysis() reports how far a ranking moves under a declared perturbation of the weights, and carries a degenerate flag, so a ranking whose alternatives were tied from the start reports that tie in place of stability.
Each method’s implementation had to agree with an independent computation of the same method on the same matrix before it was accepted. That practice caught a real defect during development, a WASPAS runner that had inherited SMART’s normalisation step by mistake.

title: surveyframe 0.4.0 is on CRAN
text:
Text analysis for open-ended responses
Open-ended answers are usually the part of a survey left unanalysed. 0.4.0 adds a 9-method family for them, running through the same analysis-plan and reporting pipeline as every other method:

term_freq and ngram_freq, top terms and top bigrams or trigrams, as a bar chart or word cloud
term_context, a keyword-in-context concordance showing what came before and after a chosen word
co_occurrence and co_occurrence_network, pairwise co-occurrence as a heatmap and a clustered force-directed network
tidy_sentiment, positive and negative counts and the proportion positive
quanteda_dfm, a document-feature matrix summary
topic_model_lda and stm_topics, Latent Dirichlet Allocation and structural topic modelling

A shared cleaning step, clean_text_responses(), and a 174-word English stopword list are both exported, so a study can reuse or override them outside a runner. The heavier methods keep their dependencies optional.
The vignette lists what the family leaves out: stemming, lemmatisation, tf-idf and keyness comparison.

title: surveyframe 0.4.0 is on CRAN
text:
Corrections for small samples
Applied research usually runs on fewer respondents than the textbook assumes, and the ordinary versions of these tests can flip significance on repeated draws from data whose true difference stayed the same. This release adds:

The Hodges-Lehmann shift estimator, for the two-group Mann-Whitney comparison
The paired Wilcoxon pseudomedian confidence interval, for the paired t-test
The exact odds-ratio confidence interval on Fisher’s test, which avoids the continuity correction a Wald interval needs when a cell is zero
Firth’s bias-reduced logistic regression, for regression prone to separation at small n

An advisory on assumption_report() and sample_size_plan() flags when a study’s sample size falls in the range where these are worth considering.

title: surveyframe 0.4.0 is on CRAN
section: Disclosed amendments and a provenance trail
text:
Disclosed amendments and a provenance trail
A SHA-256 hash proves a .sframe file is unchanged since it was written. A legitimate revision and an undisclosed edit break the hash identically, so the hash alone treats them the same.
0.4.0 adds a disclosed-revision path alongside the hash check, which keeps its full strength. amend_sframe() compares an instrument before and after a change and appends a timestamped entry to an ordered log, keeping every earlier entry. Each entry records a reason from a controlled vocabulary, a free-text explanation and which top-level fields changed.
Amendments come in 2 tiers. Pipeline amendments, such as a data correction or bot-response removal, need only a reason. Design amendments, meaning anything touching the analysis plan or a model, require a deviation report describing what changed in the research question, method, or model and why. The sign-off field is always filled. It records a reviewer’s name or the literal none, so an unreviewed design change stays visible to anyone auditing the file.
link_git_commit() records the current Git commit SHA and subject line alongside an instrument, tying the file hash to a commit that already has an explanation attached. Git is optional.
An edit made directly to a .sframe file, bypassing amend_sframe(), still fails the integrity check on read exactly as it did before.
The .sframe format is now documented as a standalone JSON Schema, so a reviewer or a second tool can validate a file with the schema alone.

title: surveyframe 0.4.0 is on CRAN
text:
What breaks
Two changes need attention before you upgrade.
validate_sframe() and validate_model() now return an sframe_validation diagnostic object, visibly, whatever the value of strict. Reading $valid and $problems still works, so the common pattern needs no migration. What breaks is code using the return value as an instrument, as in instrument <- validate_sframe(instrument). Wrap it in as_sframe(). Passing a validation result where an instrument is expected now raises an error that names the fix.
The Shiny collector now emits one expansion column per matrix cell, where it used to pipe-join a matrix item’s cells into a single column.
Both changes came out of a code review by a Journal of Statistical Software editor. The same review prompted accessor methods for every class, so user code works through methods and leaves the underlying list alone. The registered S3 method count went from 41 to 103.

title: Persona Builder: a free browser tool for personas
text: TL;DR: Persona Builder is a free, single-page browser tool for building UX research and marketing personas. Fill in a form at one of three detail levels, basic, standard or full and watch a formatted persona card update as you type. Export the finished card as a PNG or a PDF. Everything you type stays in your own browser, form data and saved personas alike. Try it at flairmi.com/tools/persona-builder.

title: Persona Builder: a free browser tool for personas
text:
Why a persona builder
A persona is a short, structured description of a type of user or customer, built from research, and used to keep a team’s decisions tied to a real audience. The idea is standard practice in UX research and marketing, but the tools for producing one tend to sit at two extremes. A blank slide offers little structure and a different result each time. A heavyweight product asks for a sign-up, a subscription or an account before the first field.
Persona Builder sits between those two. It is a form on one side of the screen and a live preview of the finished card on the other. There is no account, no subscription and no server involved once the page has loaded.

title: Persona Builder: a free browser tool for personas
text:
Three levels of detail
Personas need different amounts of information, so the tool offers 3 tiers:

Basic: name, role and a one-line summary. Enough for a quick workshop exercise or an early sketch.
Standard: adds age, location, occupation, goals, pain points, typical behaviour and preferred channels. This is the level most research and marketing teams settle on for day-to-day use.
Full: adds a representative quote, motivations, personality traits, technology comfort, key metrics tracked and a notes field for sources and caveats.

Switching levels keeps what you have already written. Fields from a lower tier stay filled in if you move up to a fuller one, and moving back down hides the extra fields, with their contents kept.

title: Persona Builder: a free browser tool for personas
text:
Avatars without a photo library
Every persona card needs a face, but real research personas are usually composites of more than one person. Persona Builder gives you three ways to fill the avatar: upload your own photo, pick one of eight generated sample avatars, or fall back to plain initials. The sample avatars are drawn as inline SVG shapes at the point you click them, so the page loads them with zero external requests.

title: Persona Builder: a free browser tool for personas
text:
Export and save
A finished card exports as a PNG or a PDF with one click, sized for dropping straight into a slide deck or a research report. Personas can also be saved inside the tool itself for later editing, a saved list appears under the form with each entry’s name and last-updated date, and any entry can be reloaded or deleted. Saved data lives in the browser’s local storage on the device you are using, so it stays on that device and away from any server.

title: Why the analysis plan comes first
text: TL;DR: If you decide how to analyse a survey after you have seen the responses, you will tend to find the answer you were hoping for, even with the best intentions. surveyframe asks you to write the analysis plan into the instrument before you collect anything, and then it runs that plan as declared. This post explains why that order is worth the small extra effort, for readers who run surveys.

title: Why the analysis plan comes first
section: The usual order, and the problem with it
text:
The usual order, and the problem with it
Here is how most survey work goes. You write the questions, send the survey out, wait for responses, and then open the results and start looking. You try one comparison, then another. You drop the two respondents who clearly rushed. You split by region because the overall number looked flat. Somewhere in there you find something that reaches significance, and that becomes the finding you report.
Each step in that story is a reasonable choice a careful person might make. The problem is that many reasonable choices were available, and you made them after seeing which ones pointed somewhere interesting. When the number of paths is large, at least one of them will look like a result by chance alone. Choosing the path after seeing the data quietly stacks the odds in favour of finding something, real or otherwise.
This is the everyday way survey results are produced, and it helps explain why so many survey findings fail to replicate.

title: Why the analysis plan comes first
text:
The order surveyframe uses instead
surveyframe changes the order. The analysis plan is part of the instrument you build, and you build the instrument before you collect data. You state which questions form which scale, how they are scored, which groups you will compare and which test answers each question. That plan is written down before any response exists.
When the data arrives, surveyframe runs the plan you declared. The comparisons you committed to are the comparisons you get. You can explore further, and the pre-declared result stays on its own, clearly separate from anything you went looking for afterwards.
Exploration stays open to you. What changes is that the plan fixed in advance holds its shape, because it was fixed before you could see what you found.

title: Why the analysis plan comes first
text:
Why this matters outside academia
This reads like a concern for journals and peer review, yet the same trap sits inside ordinary commercial survey work.
Suppose you run a brand survey and want to know whether a campaign shifted how people feel. If you decide what counts as a shift after seeing the numbers, you can almost always describe some slice of the data as a win. That reads well in a deck. The next campaign, judged the same loose way, will look like a win too, and you lose the chance to learn which campaigns worked. A plan fixed in advance lets a real effect and a lucky slice look different from each other, and that is worth money as well as methodological tidiness.

title: Why the analysis plan comes first
text:
The integrity angle
A stronger version of this idea is where surveyframe is heading. If the instrument and its analysis plan are fixed before data collection, you can make that fact verifiable, so that anyone reading the results can confirm the plan stayed as declared. The methodology behind that is set out in a companion preprint, Social Science Research 6.0: A Proof-of-Integrity Framework for Tamper-Evident Survey Instruments. Read it if you want to prove, with evidence, that you called your shot in advance.

title: Why the analysis plan comes first
text:
Where the methods go next
Declaring a plan in advance is more demanding with a small sample, the situation most applied researchers work in. Large-sample rules of thumb fall away, and every analytic choice carries more weight. surveyframe 0.4 added small-sample corrections for that case, and the reasoning is set out in the companion textbook, Quantitative Analysis with Small Samples, which is free to read.

title: Why the analysis plan comes first
text:
Try it
surveyframe is on CRAN. You can install it and build an instrument in one line:
install.packages("surveyframe")
The latest release notes are in surveyframe 0.4.1 on CRAN, and the full documentation is at mohammedalisharafuddin.github.io/surveyframe.

title: Logistic Regression Basics: Predicting Purchase from Session Count
text:
Case
You are analysing customer behaviour for an e-commerce platform and want to understand: Does the number of on-site sessions influence the likelihood of making a purchase? Specifically, how much do purchase odds increase with each additional session? Can you predict purchase probability from session count to identify high-intent customers?

title: Logistic Regression Basics: Predicting Purchase from Session Count
text:
Method
We use logistic regression to model the relationship between session count (predictor) and purchase outcome (binary response). Unlike linear regression, logistic regression models the log-odds (logit) of the outcome:
\[
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Sessions},
\]
where \(p\) is the probability of purchase. Rearranging gives the predicted probability:
\[
p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Sessions})}}.
\]
The odds ratio (OR) for a one-unit increase in sessions is: \[
\text{OR} = e^{\beta_1}.
\]
An OR > 1 indicates increased odds of purchase with more sessions, and an OR < 1 indicates decreased odds. We report 95% Wald confidence intervals for the odds ratio.
Interpretation guide: - OR = 1.00: No effect - OR = 1.31: 31% increase in odds per additional session - OR = 2.00: 100% increase (doubling) in odds - OR = 0.80: 20% decrease in odds

title: Logistic Regression Basics: Predicting Purchase from Session Count
text:
Results and Interpretation
The logistic regression reveals a statistically significant positive relationship between session count and purchase probability. The estimated slope coefficient is β₁ = 0.268 (SE = 0.035, z = 7.58, p < .001), which translates to an odds ratio of 1.31 (95% CI [1.22, 1.40]) (R Core Team 2024).
Odds ratio interpretation: For every additional session, the odds of making a purchase increase by 31%. Customers with 2 sessions have 1.31 times the odds of purchasing of customers with 1 session, holding all else constant. The 95% CI [1.22, 1.40] places the true effect between a 22% and a 40% increase in odds per session.
Probability predictions: - 1 session: Predicted purchase probability = 14.2% - 3 sessions (mean): Predicted purchase probability = 22.0% - 5 sessions: Predicted purchase probability = 32.6% - 8 sessions: Predicted purchase probability = 51.9%
The model shows purchase probability increases non-linearly with sessions, following a logistic S-curve. Customers with 4 or more sessions pass 25% purchase probability, against about 14% for single-session visitors. Overall, 23.2% of the 1,500 customers bought.
Model fit: The McFadden pseudo R² of 0.036 (3.6%) indicates the model explains a modest portion of variance in purchase outcomes. This is typical for individual-level behavioural models where pseudo R² values of 2-15% are often acceptable, because many factors beyond session count influence purchase decisions. The residual deviance (1,565.9) is lower than the null deviance (1,625.0) by 59.1 on 1 degree of freedom, so the model improves clearly on the intercept-only baseline.
Statistical significance: The Wald z-test for the slope, z = 7.58, p < .001, gives strong evidence that session count predicts purchase probability.
Decision framework. The positive relationship between sessions and purchase probability suggests 5 actionable steps: (1) Engagement strategies: Encourage multi-session visits through retargeting, email reminders or personalised recommendations, (2) Customer segmentation: Treat 1-session visitors differently from 5+ session visitors in targeting and messaging, (3) Lead scoring: Use session count as a component of lead quality scores, (4) Conversion optimisation: Focus conversion tactics on high-session users who show strongest purchase intent (>25% probability), (5) Further analysis: Extend the model with additional predictors (device type, traffic source, time on site) to improve predictions and understand interaction effects.

title: Logistic Regression Basics: Predicting Purchase from Session Count
text:
Assumptions
Logistic regression assumes:

Binary outcome: Purchase is coded as 0 (no purchase) or 1 (purchase)
Independence: Each customer’s purchase decision is independent of others
Linearity of log-odds: The relationship between sessions and log-odds of purchase is linear (can test with polynomial terms)
Overlap between outcomes: Every session count includes both buyers and non-buyers, so the predictor leaves the outcomes overlapping
Large sample size: Generally requires n ≥ 10 events per predictor (1,500 observations with 1 predictor is adequate)

Note: Normal residuals and homoscedasticity are linear-regression assumptions, and logistic regression drops both.

title: Logistic Regression Basics: Predicting Purchase from Session Count
text:
Limitations
This analysis leaves out:

Confounding variables: Device type, traffic source, time spent per session, page views, product browsing behaviour
Time effects: Session timing (same day vs. spread over weeks), recency effects, seasonality
Customer heterogeneity: New vs. returning customers, demographics, purchase history
Non-linear effects: Diminishing returns at very high session counts (may plateau beyond 8-10 sessions)
Model calibration: Predicted probabilities need validation on held-out data before they can be trusted
Interaction effects: Session impact may vary by customer segment or traffic source
Causality: Correlation stops short of proving that sessions cause purchases. High-intent customers may naturally browse more.

Recommendations for improvement: - Add categorical predictors (device type, traffic source) and test interactions with sessions - Include continuous predictors (average time per session, pages viewed, cart additions) - Test polynomial terms (sessions²) or splines for non-linear relationships - Split data into training/test sets to assess out-of-sample prediction accuracy - Calculate AUC-ROC and calibration curves to evaluate discrimination and calibration - Consider hierarchical models if sessions are nested within customers over time - Use propensity score matching or causal inference methods to estimate treatment effects

title: Welch t-Test vs Equal-Variance t-Test: Comparing Methods
text:
Method
We compare two approaches to testing differences in means:

Equal-variance t-test (Student’s t-test): Assumes both groups have equal population variances and pools sample variances to estimate standard error
Welch t-test: Allows the variances to differ and adjusts degrees of freedom to the variance ratio (Welch 1947)

The Welch t-test is generally more robust when variances differ, especially with unequal sample sizes. We calculate the variance ratio (smaller variance / larger variance) to assess heterogeneity. A ratio below 0.5, meaning one variance is more than twice the other, suggests meaningful variance differences and strongly favours the Welch t-test.
Test statistic for equal-variance t-test: \[
t = \frac{\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_A} + \frac{1}{n_B}}}, \quad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_A-1)s_A^2 + (n_B-1)s_B^2}{n_A + n_B - 2}.
\]
Test statistic for Welch t-test: \[
t = \frac{\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B}{\sqrt{\frac{s_A^2}{n_A} + \frac{s_B^2}{n_B}}}, \quad df \approx \frac{\left(\frac{s_A^2}{n_A} + \frac{s_B^2}{n_B}\right)^2}{\frac{(s_A^2/n_A)^2}{n_A-1} + \frac{(s_B^2/n_B)^2}{n_B-1}}.
\]

title: Welch t-Test vs Equal-Variance t-Test: Comparing Methods
text:
Results and Interpretation
Group A had a mean AOV of ₹1,203.5 (SD = ₹151.4, n=120), while group B had a mean AOV of ₹1,281.7 (SD = ₹290.5, n=150). The variance ratio of 0.27 (22,919 / 84,416) shows group B’s variance is nearly 4 times group A’s, which strongly favours the Welch t-test.
Welch t-test results: The Welch t-test found a statistically significant difference, t(233.6) = 2.85, p = .005, with a 95% CI of [₹24.0, ₹132.2] for the mean difference (B − A) (Welch 1947; R Core Team 2024). The adjusted degrees of freedom (233.6 against the pooled 268) reflect the variance inequality.
Equal-variance t-test results: The equal-variance t-test gave t(268) = 2.67, p = .008, with a 95% CI of [₹20.5, ₹135.7]. The 2 tests agree here, but the equal-variance assumption is violated (variance ratio 0.27, below 0.5).
Method comparison: When variances differ substantially and sample sizes are unequal, the equal-variance t-test gives the wrong error rate. It is too liberal when the smaller group has the larger variance, and too conservative when, as here, the larger group has it. The Welch t-test keeps the error rate close to 5% either way. Both tests reach the same conclusion here (p < .05), and Welch is the result to report.
Decision framework. With a variance ratio of 0.27 and unequal sample sizes, use the Welch t-test as your primary result. The mean difference of ₹78 (95% CI [₹24, ₹132]) shows group B has the higher AOV, and the wide interval leaves the size of that gap uncertain. Check variance homogeneity before choosing your test, and default to Welch when in doubt, since it holds up even when the variances are equal.

title: Welch t-Test vs Equal-Variance t-Test: Comparing Methods
text:
Sample Size Planning
For future tests with similar variance structure, plan for adequate power using the more conservative Welch approach. To detect a ₹70 difference with 80% power at α = 0.05 (assuming the larger SD, about ₹260), you need about 217 per group (434 total), or 290 per group for 90% power. Planned this way, the current test, with 120 and 150 customers, had about 57% power for a difference of ₹68.

Note: When planning with unequal variances, use the larger standard deviation for conservative sample size estimates. Equal sample sizes are preferable as they maximise power and minimise Type I error inflation.

title: Welch t-Test vs Equal-Variance t-Test: Comparing Methods
text:
Assumptions
Both t-tests assume:

Independent observations: Each customer’s order is independent
Random sampling: Customers were randomly sampled from their respective populations
Approximate normality: AOV distributions are approximately normal, or sample sizes are large enough (n ≥ 30 per group) for the Central Limit Theorem to apply

Additional assumption for equal-variance t-test: - Homogeneity of variance: Population variances are equal (violated here, with a ratio of 0.27)
Welch t-test advantage: Works with unequal variances, adjusting degrees of freedom automatically to the observed variance ratio.

title: Welch t-Test vs Equal-Variance t-Test: Comparing Methods
text:
Limitations
This analysis leaves out:

Levene’s test or F-test: We used variance ratio as a rule of thumb (< 0.5 or > 2.0). Formal tests like Levene’s test can assess homogeneity statistically
Non-normality: With smaller samples or extreme skewness, consider non-parametric alternatives (Mann-Whitney U test)
Paired data: For paired measurements, use the paired t-test
Multiple groups: For more than two groups, use ANOVA with appropriate variance adjustments (Welch ANOVA)

When variance ratio is between 0.5 and 2.0 with equal sample sizes, both tests typically give similar results. Always report which test you used and justify the choice based on variance diagnostics.

Method
We use a two-proportion z test to compare independent proportions (Agresti 2019). The test statistic follows a chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom when using the squared z statistic. We report the difference with a 95% confidence interval and Cohen’s h as an effect size measure.
The difference in proportions: \[
\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B = \frac{x_A}{n_A} - \frac{x_B}{n_B}.
\]
Cohen’s h for effect size: \[
h = 2(\arcsin\sqrt{\hat{p}_A} - \arcsin\sqrt{\hat{p}_B}).
\]

title: Two-Proportion Test: Comparing Conversion Rates Between Variants

Assumptions
The two-proportion test assumes:

Independent samples: Each visitor appears in only one variant (no crossover or contamination between groups)
Random assignment: Visitors were randomly allocated to A or B without systematic bias (e.g., no assignment based on time of day or device type)
Large sample approximation: Each group has at least 5 expected successes and 5 expected failures for the normal approximation to hold (both conditions met: 120 successes and 880 failures in A, 95 successes and 905 failures in B, all above 5)
Stable conversion rates: The true conversion rate for each variant remains constant during the test period (no external events or time trends affecting one group differently)

Method
We use a Welch t-test to compare two independent groups with potentially unequal variances (Welch 1947). This is more robust than Student’s t-test when variances differ. We report the mean difference with a 95% confidence interval and Hedges g as an effect size measure (which applies a small-sample correction to Cohen’s d).
The mean difference: \[
\bar{x}_B - \bar{x}_A = \frac{1}{n_B}\sum x_{B,i} - \frac{1}{n_A}\sum x_{A,i}.
\]
Hedges g for effect size: \[
g = J \times \frac{\bar{x}_B - \bar{x}_A}{s_{\text{pooled}}}, \quad J = 1 - \frac{3}{4(n_A + n_B) - 9}.
\]

To detect an ₹80 difference in AOV, the lift the experiment was designed around, with 80% power at α = 0.05 (assuming SD ≈ ₹280), you need about 193 customers per group (386 total), or 258 per group for 90% power. The current test, with 200 per group, had about 81% power for that ₹80 difference.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
For future tests, use the formula: \[
n_{\text{per group}} = \frac{2(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2}{d^2},
\] where \(d\) is Cohen’s d (mean difference divided by pooled standard deviation).

title: Welch t-Test: Comparing Average Order Value Between Groups
text:
Assumptions
The Welch t-test assumes:

Independent observations: Each customer’s order is independent
Random assignment: Customers were randomly allocated to control or treatment
Approximate normality: AOV distributions are approximately normal, or sample sizes are large enough (n ≥ 30 per group) for the Central Limit Theorem to apply
Unequal variances allowed: The Welch t-test adjusts its degrees of freedom for unequal variances (SD control = ₹279, treatment = ₹296)

title: Welch t-Test: Comparing Average Order Value Between Groups
text:
Limitations
This analysis leaves out:

Skewness: AOV distributions in retail are often right-skewed. Consider median comparisons or log-transformation if extreme outliers are present.
Segmentation: Results may vary by customer segment (new vs. returning, device type, traffic source)
Time effects: Seasonal patterns or time-of-week effects could influence AOV
Multiple testing: If running multiple simultaneous experiments, adjust significance levels accordingly

For highly skewed data, consider the Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) as a non-parametric alternative.

text: TL;DR: Revenue = ₹47.9k + ₹0.31 per ₹1 ad spend (n=200 weeks), slope CI [₹0.16, ₹0.45], R² = 0.08 (weak fit), residuals look normal. Decision: the link is real but small. Each ₹1k of ad spend brings back about ₹306 of revenue, less than it costs.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Modelling Revenue from Ad Spend
text:
Case
You manage digital advertising for an e-commerce platform and want to quantify the relationship between weekly ad spend and revenue. Specifically: For every additional rupee spent on ads, how much revenue can you expect? Is the relationship strong enough to justify continued investment? What portion of revenue variation is explained by ad spend alone?

title: Simple Linear Regression: Modelling Revenue from Ad Spend
text:
Method
We use ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to model revenue as a linear function of ad spend. The regression equation is:
\[
\text{Revenue}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Spend}_i + \epsilon_i,
\]
where \(\beta_0\) is the intercept (baseline revenue when spend = 0), \(\beta_1\) is the slope (marginal revenue per rupee of spend), and \(\epsilon_i\) is the error term assumed to be normally distributed with constant variance.
The slope estimate with standard error: \[
\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \quad SE(\hat{\beta}_1) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}},
\] where \(s\) is the residual standard error.
The coefficient of determination (R-squared): \[
R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{\text{res}}}{SS_{\text{tot}}} = 1 - \frac{\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2}.
\]
We report 95% confidence intervals for both intercept and slope using standard t-distribution critical values.

title: Simple Linear Regression: Modelling Revenue from Ad Spend
text:
Results and Interpretation
The regression analysis reveals a statistically significant positive relationship between ad spend and revenue. The estimated slope is ₹0.306 (95% CI [₹0.164, ₹0.447]), meaning that for every additional rupee spent on advertising, revenue increases by about ₹0.31 on average, b = 0.306, SE = 0.072, t(198) = 4.26, p < .001 (R Core Team 2024).
The intercept of ₹47,899 (95% CI [₹39,517, ₹56,281]) is the estimated baseline revenue when ad spend is zero. Read it with care, since the model describes the observed spend range of ₹0 to ₹100,000 and nothing beyond it.
Model fit: The R² value of 0.084 (8%) indicates that ad spend explains about 8% of the variation in weekly revenue (adjusted R² = 0.079). The other 92% comes from factors outside this simple model, such as seasonality, competitor actions, organic traffic and product mix. The residual standard error of ₹29,674 shows how widely weekly revenue scatters around the line.
Statistical significance: The F-statistic, F(1, 198) = 18.12, p < .001, confirms the model is significant. The relationship is real but small.
Practical significance: Each extra rupee of spend brings back about ₹0.31 of revenue, and the 95% CI [₹0.16, ₹0.45] stays below ₹1. On these numbers, extra ad spend returns less revenue than it costs, before any other costs are subtracted.
Decision framework. The relationship is significant, yet the marginal return falls short of the spend, and association alone is weak evidence of cause. Before making budget decisions: (1) Check residual diagnostics for violations of regression assumptions, (2) Consider confounding variables (e.g., seasonality, external events), (3) Calculate net profit impact after subtracting ad costs and other variable costs, (4) Test whether the relationship holds at different spend levels (non-linearity), (5) Consider building a multiple regression model with additional predictors for better prediction accuracy.

Residual Diagnostics

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Diagnostic interpretation: The residuals vs. fitted plot should show random scatter around zero (no pattern). The Q-Q plot should show points following the diagonal line. Deviations suggest violations of assumptions (heteroscedasticity, non-normality or non-linearity).

title: Simple Linear Regression: Modelling Revenue from Ad Spend
text:
Assumptions
Simple linear regression assumes:

Linearity: The relationship between spend and revenue is linear (check with scatterplot and residual plot)
Independence: Weekly observations are independent (no autocorrelation across time)
Homoscedasticity: Constant variance of residuals across all levels of spend (check residuals vs. fitted plot)
Normality of residuals: Residuals are approximately normally distributed (check the Q-Q plot, less critical with n = 200)
Accurate predictor: Ad spend is measured accurately
Unconfounded predictor: Other important predictors are uncorrelated with spend

title: Simple Linear Regression: Modelling Revenue from Ad Spend
text:
Limitations
This analysis leaves out:

Causality: Correlation stops short of proving that ad spend causes revenue. Reverse causality is possible (higher revenue allows more ad spend)
Confounding variables: Seasonality, promotions, competitor actions, product launches, organic trends
Non-linear relationships: Diminishing returns at high spend levels, or threshold effects at low spend
Time series structure: Temporal autocorrelation, lagged effects (ads may influence future weeks)
Interaction effects: Ad effectiveness may vary by channel, audience segment or time period
Costs: This models revenue, not profit. Must subtract ad costs and variable costs to assess true ROI

Recommendations for improvement: - Add time trends and seasonal dummies to control for temporal patterns - Use multiple regression with additional predictors (organic traffic, email campaigns, competitor spend) - Test for non-linearity with polynomial terms or segmented regression - Consider time series models (ARIMA, VAR) if temporal dependencies exist - Conduct controlled experiments (randomized ad spend levels) to establish causality - Calculate contribution margin and customer lifetime value for profit-focused analysis

title: surveyframe 0.3.3 is on CRAN
text: TL;DR: surveyframe 0.3.3 was accepted on CRAN on 11 July 2026. Install it with install.packages("surveyframe"). The full documentation site is now live at mohammedalisharafuddin.github.io/surveyframe. This release rebuilds the look of the exported survey, meets WCAG 2.2 AA, reflows properly on phones and adds an opt-in ggplot2 plotting layer including a diverging stacked-bar chart for Likert results. It is free and open source under the MIT licence.

title: surveyframe 0.3.3 is on CRAN
text:
What surveyframe is
surveyframe is an R package for survey research. Its one distinctive idea is the order of work. You build the instrument first, which means the questions, the scoring rules and the analysis plan, and you do that before you collect a single response. The plan you declare up front is the plan that runs when the data comes in.
Most survey tools work the other way round. You gather responses, open the results, and then decide how to analyse them. surveyframe makes that harder to do by accident, because the analysis is already written down as part of the instrument. That is worth explaining on its own, so it gets its own post.

title: surveyframe 0.3.3 is on CRAN
text:
Install it
install.packages("surveyframe")
That is the whole install. surveyframe is on CRAN, so there is no extra step and no development toolchain to set up. The documentation, function reference and worked examples now live on the pkgdown site.

title: surveyframe 0.3.3 is on CRAN
text:
What is new in 0.3.3

The exported survey looks like a real instrument
The survey you export has been redesigned end to end. Question text now uses larger serif typography, options sit in bordered cards with a selection tick, Likert points are numbered squares, and the matrix, slider and ranking blocks have all been restyled. A slim progress bar runs along the top. The result reads as a considered survey, and that matters when you are asking real respondents to give you real attention.


It meets WCAG 2.2 AA
The exported survey passes an instrumented accessibility audit at WCAG 2.2 AA. In practice that means every input carries an accessible name, keyboard focus is visible as you move across the option cards, and validation errors are announced to assistive technology as well as shown in colour. Required questions are marked in more than one way, ranking items can be reordered with the keyboard, and touch targets meet a 44-pixel minimum on phones. Accessibility here is a property the build checks.


It works on a phone
Matrix questions used to force a wide table that needed horizontal scrolling on a small screen. Below 600 pixels they now reflow into stacked, labelled row cards, so a respondent on a phone answers the same question with a simple scroll.


A plotting layer, on request
There is a new optional plotting layer built on ggplot2. Turn it on and your analysis blocks gain charts: bar charts for frequency and chi-square blocks, and scatter plots with a regression overlay for correlation and regression blocks. It is opt-in, so your reports change only when you ask for it.


A proper chart for Likert scales
Likert items in a report now get a diverging stacked-bar chart. Agreement and disagreement diverge from the centre, darkest at each pole and lightest next to the neutral point, so you can read the balance of a scale at a glance.

title: surveyframe 0.3.3 is on CRAN
text:
Built from a real study
surveyframe 0.3.3 was hardened while running a live survey study on AI room service. That deployment surfaced a real bug: the submission call to Google Apps Script was triggering a CORS preflight that Apps Script leaves unanswered, so some responses were being dropped silently. The submission path has been rewritten to avoid that preflight, and those responses now arrive. Bugs found in production matter most, and this release fixes the ones the study found.

title: surveyframe 0.3.3 is on CRAN
text:
Where it is heading
The next version, v0.4, leans into small-sample methods, the situation most applied researchers face. That work is anchored by the companion textbook, Quantitative Analysis with Small Samples, which is free and already available. A manuscript describing the package has also been submitted to the Journal of Statistical Software and is under review. More on that if and when it is accepted.

title: surveyframe Field Types: Single Choice
text: TL;DR: single_choice captures one answer from a fixed list. This post declares one with sf_item(), shows the real codebook table it produces, the real exported question a respondent sees, and the real frequency table and chart that come out the other end when responses arrive. Every table and chart on this page, except the one screenshot of the exported survey, was generated by the R code shown, at render time, from surveyframe 0.3.3.

title: surveyframe Field Types: Single Choice
text:
The case
You run a small store and want to know one thing about each visitor before you ask anything else: have they been here before? That single fact changes how you should read every other answer they give you. It is a single_choice question, because every visitor is exactly one of 2 things: a first-time visitor or a repeat visitor.

title: surveyframe Field Types: Single Choice
text:
Declare the item
A single_choice item needs an id, a label, a choice_set, and whether it is required. The choice set is declared separately with sf_choices() and referenced by its id.

choices <- sf_choices(
  "visit_freq",
  values = c("first", "repeat"),
  labels = c("First-time visitor", "Repeat visitor")
)

item <- sf_item(
  id = "visitor_type",
  label = "How would you describe your visit today?",
  type = "single_choice",
  choice_set = "visit_freq",
  required = TRUE
)

instrument <- sf_instrument(
  title = "Store Visit Survey",
  version = "0.1.0",
  components = list(choices, item)
)

That is the whole instrument for now: one choice set, one item. Everything below reads from this instrument object, typed once.

section: Write the analysis plan before you collect anything
text:
Write the analysis plan before you collect anything
Do this part deliberately. The plan below is declared now, attached to the instrument, before a single response exists. method = "frequency" with roles = list(variable = "visitor_type") tells surveyframe which table and chart to produce later. Why this order matters is its own post if you want the fuller argument.

instrument <- sf_instrument(
  title = "Store Visit Survey",
  version = "0.1.0",
  components = list(choices, item),
  analysis_plan = list(
    list(
      id = "RQ1",
      research_question = "What proportion of visitors today are repeat visitors?",
      family = "descriptive_categorical",
      method = "frequency",
      roles = list(variable = "visitor_type")
    )
  )
)

title: surveyframe Field Types: Multiple Choice
text: TL;DR: multiple_choice lets a respondent select any number of options at once, a nominal set of answers. This post declares one with sf_item(), shows the real codebook and exported survey, then runs a real Cochran’s Q test to check whether selection rates differ across options, alongside the multi-response summary table every “select all that apply” question needs. Every table and chart on this page, except the one screenshot of the exported survey, was generated by the R code shown, at render time, from surveyframe 0.3.4 installed straight from CRAN.

title: surveyframe Field Types: Multiple Choice
text:
The case
You run a small store and just finished a promotion across 5 channels: Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, an email newsletter and in-store signage. You want to know which of those channels people noticed, and a visitor may have noticed more than one. That calls for more than single_choice, since forcing one answer would throw away real information. It is a multiple_choice question: select all that apply.

title: surveyframe Field Types: Multiple Choice
text:
Declare the item
A multiple_choice item is declared exactly like single_choice: an id, a label, a choice_set, and whether it is required. The difference lies in how a respondent answers it and how the responses come back.

choices <- sf_choices(
  "channels_used",
  values = c("instagram", "facebook", "tiktok", "email", "in_store"),
  labels = c("Instagram", "Facebook", "TikTok", "Email newsletter", "In-store signage")
)

item <- sf_item(
  id = "channels_used",
  label = "Which of these did you notice our store's promotion on? Select all that apply.",
  type = "multiple_choice",
  choice_set = "channels_used",
  required = TRUE
)

instrument <- sf_instrument(
  title = "Promotion Awareness Survey",
  version = "0.1.0",
  components = list(choices, item)
)

title: surveyframe Field Types: Multiple Choice
section: Write the analysis plan before you collect anything
text:
Write the analysis plan before you collect anything
A single multiple_choice item comes back as one column per option, each TRUE or FALSE, since a respondent can tick any combination of the five. The frequency method from the single_choice post only tabulates one variable at a time, so this item needs a different method: run frequency on 5 binary columns and it tabulates the first one alone, dropping the other 4. Keep that in mind before you rely on it.
The method built for exactly this shape is cochran_q: it tests whether the selection rate differs across a set of related binary measures. Declared with roles = list(measures = ...), naming every column, before any response exists.

instrument <- sf_instrument(
  title = "Promotion Awareness Survey",
  version = "0.1.0",
  components = list(choices, item),
  analysis_plan = list(
    list(
      id = "RQ1",
      research_question = "Do selection rates differ across the five channels?",
      family = "association",
      method = "cochran_q",
      roles = list(measures = c(
        "channels_used_instagram", "channels_used_facebook", "channels_used_tiktok",
        "channels_used_email", "channels_used_in_store"
      ))
    )
  )
)

The exact file is downloadable as 11-multiple-choice-responses.csv, if you would rather point read_responses() at a real file than regenerate it.

set.seed(42)
n <- 140
responses <- data.frame(
  channels_used_instagram = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.45)),
  channels_used_facebook  = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.35, 0.65)),
  channels_used_tiktok    = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.40, 0.60)),
  channels_used_email     = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.20, 0.80)),
  channels_used_in_store  = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.15, 0.85))
)

rq1 <- results[[1]]

That result answers one question: are the 5 rates different at all. Which channel leads, and by how much, is the next question and the one a reader wants answered first.

title: surveyframe 0.4.1 is on CRAN
text:
A library of 22 demos
The most common question about a survey package is which approach fits the data you have.

title: 7Ps Marketing Mix Planner
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What are the 7Ps of marketing?
    The 7Ps of marketing are product, price, place, promotion, people, process and physical evidence. Booms and Bitner (1981) added the last three to the original four Ps because services depend on the staff, the steps customers go through and the tangible cues they see.
  
  
    What is the difference between the 4Ps and the 7Ps?
    The 4Ps cover product, price, place and promotion and suit physical goods. The 7Ps add people, process and physical evidence, which matter whenever a service is produced and consumed at the same time, as in hotels, banking and education.
  
  
    How do you check a marketing mix is consistent?
    Test each P against the positioning statement. This planner rates every P from 1 to 5 for how well it supports the positioning and flags the lowest as the weakest link.
  
  
    What is a 7Ps example for a hotel?
    For business travellers: a quiet room with a desk (product), a member rate below the public rate (price), direct booking and a corporate travel desk (place), a know-before-you-book message (promotion), staff able to waive fees (people), mobile check-in (process) and Wi-Fi speed shown at booking (physical evidence).

How it works

title: Ansoff Matrix Tool
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is the Ansoff Matrix?
    The Ansoff Matrix is a growth planning grid that crosses existing and new products with existing and new markets. It gives four strategies, in rising order of risk: market penetration, market development, product development and diversification.
  
  
    Which Ansoff strategy is the riskiest?
    Diversification is the riskiest, because a new product in a new market means the business knows neither the customers nor the offer. Market penetration is the least risky and usually has the lowest growth ceiling.
  
  
    How does this Ansoff tool score risk?
    It scores product newness and market newness from 0 to 10 for each initiative. Risk is the mean of the two scaled to 100, so an initiative that is half new on both axes scores 50.
  
  
    What is an example of the Ansoff Matrix?
    For a hotel group, loyalty tiers for current guests are market penetration, opening in Porto is market development, wellness packages are product development and a booking app sold to other hotels is diversification. The tool opens on this example.
