title: BCG Growth-Share Matrix
text:
How it works
Relative market share is your share divided by the share of the largest competitor. A value of 1.0 means level with the leader, and anything above 1.0 means you lead.
Relative market share = your market share ÷ largest competitor's shareStar: growth at or above the threshold, relative share 1.0 or moreCash cow: growth below the threshold, relative share 1.0 or moreQuestion mark: growth at or above the threshold, relative share below 1.0Dog: growth below the threshold, relative share below 1.0
The horizontal axis uses a log scale with high share on the left, as in the original matrix. The growth threshold defaults to 10% and can be changed to suit the industry.

title: BCG Growth-Share Matrix
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is the BCG matrix?
    The BCG growth-share matrix is a portfolio tool from the Boston Consulting Group that plots products by market growth rate and relative market share. It sorts them into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs to show which products generate cash and which need it.
  
  
    How do you calculate relative market share?
    Divide your market share by the share of your largest competitor. A 20% share against a leader's 40% gives 0.5. A value above 1.0 means you lead the market.
  
  
    What do stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs mean?
    Stars lead growing markets and need investment to keep share. Cash cows lead slow markets and fund the rest. Question marks trail in growing markets and need a decision. Dogs trail in slow markets and are candidates to harvest or sell.
  
  
    What are the limits of the BCG matrix?
    The BCG matrix uses one measure per axis, assumes market share brings lower costs and ignores links between products. The GE-McKinsey matrix adds more factors when growth and share alone miss what matters.

    What should a marketing campaign brief include?
    A marketing campaign brief should include a dated, measurable objective, the target audience, the positioning and key message, the channels and budget split, the timeline, the KPIs and mandatories such as brand or legal rules.

title: Customer Lifetime Value Calculator
text:
How it works
The annual margin per customer is order value times purchases per year times gross margin. Retention sets the chance a customer is still buying each year, and the discount rate converts future profit to today’s value.
Annual margin m = order value × purchases per year × margin %CLV over T years = Σt=0T−1 m × rt ÷ (1 + d)tCLV over an open-ended horizon = m × (1 + d) ÷ (1 + d − r)Simple CLV = m ÷ (1 − r)
r is the retention rate and d the discount rate. A CLV to CAC ratio of 3 to 1 or more is a common benchmark for a healthy acquisition budget.

title: Customer Lifetime Value Calculator
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is customer lifetime value?
    Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the profit a customer brings over the whole relationship, stated in today's money. Set against the cost of acquiring a customer, it shows how much a business can afford to spend on acquisition.
  
  
    How do you calculate customer lifetime value?
    Multiply order value, purchases per year and gross margin to get the annual margin. Then add up each year's margin, weighted by the chance the customer is still buying and discounted to today. Over an open-ended horizon, CLV is the annual margin times (1 + d) divided by (1 + d minus r).
  
  
    What is a good CLV to CAC ratio?
    3 to 1 is a common benchmark for the CLV to CAC ratio. Much lower means acquisition costs too much. Much higher can mean the business is under-investing in growth.
  
  
    How does retention affect customer lifetime value?
    Retention compounds year on year. In the sample, raising retention from 62% to 75% lifts five-year CLV by about a quarter, from 843 to 1,051.

Each persona records what the guest wants, how they feel, and which segment they belong to at every stage. Two guests on the same journey then show as 2 separate emotion curves, and a guest who moves from one segment to another shows the stage where it happens.

title: Customer Journey Mapper
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is a customer journey map?
    A customer journey map is a visual record of the steps a customer takes with an organisation, from first awareness through purchase and use to what follows. A useful map records touchpoints, the customer's goal and emotion at each stage, and the pain points where the experience breaks.
  
  
    What are the stages of a hotel customer journey?
    A common resort model uses six stages: inspiration, research, booking, pre-arrival, on-site and post-stay. Research on luxury hotels groups the journey into pre-decision, decision and post-experience phases (O'Rourke et al., 2026).
  
  
    What is the difference between a journey map and a service blueprint?
    A journey map shows the customer's experience. A service blueprint adds what happens behind it: frontstage staff, backstage work and support processes, separated by the lines of interaction, visibility and internal interaction. This tool draws both on one page.
  
  
    Why map personas stage by stage?
    Mapping personas stage by stage shows how customers change during a journey. A fixed persona assumes the customer stays the same, yet a cautious guest can become an advocate after one well-handled moment. Recording goal, emotion and segment at each stage keeps that change visible.
  
  
    How do I use the Customer Journey Mapper in a workshop or class?
    Project the map and give each group one stage and one persona to blueprint. Each group tags pain points to a service gap and an owning silo, then exports a PNG or PDF. Save the JSON file to reopen the map later.
  
  
    Is this Customer Journey Mapper free?
    Yes. The Customer Journey Mapper is free and opens straight away in any modern browser, including on a phone. Maps are saved in your browser's local storage and stay on your device.

title: Diffusion of Innovation Adopter Calculator
text:
In progress
Rogers’ diffusion of innovations divides a market into five adopter groups by when they take up something new: innovators, early adopters, the early majority, the late majority and laggards. Each group responds to different arguments, so knowing which group you are reaching now tells you what the next campaign has to do.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. It opens on quarterly mobile check-in users across a hotel group. Enter adopters and market potential, or paste new adopters per period and fit the Bass model.

title: Diffusion of Innovation Adopter Calculator
text:
How it works
Cumulative adoption is the share of the market potential that has adopted. Rogers’ groups are bands of a normal curve: innovators are the first 2.5%, early adopters the next 13.5%, the early majority and late majority 34% each, and laggards the final 16%.
The Bass model splits adoption into two forces: innovation, people who adopt on their own, and imitation, people who adopt because others have.
n(t) = p · m + (q − p) · N(t−1) − (q ÷ m) · N(t−1)²p = innovation coefficient, q = imitation coefficient, m = market potentialPeak adoption at t* = ln(q ÷ p) ÷ (p + q)
The coefficients are estimated by ordinary least squares on new adopters against cumulative adopters, the method in Bass (1969).

title: Diffusion of Innovation Adopter Calculator
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is the diffusion of innovations theory?
    Diffusion of innovations, from Everett Rogers (1962), explains how new products spread through a market. Adopters fall into five groups by when they adopt: innovators, early adopters, the early majority, the late majority and laggards.
  
  
    What percentage is each adopter category?
    Innovators are 2.5% of eventual adopters, early adopters 13.5%, the early majority 34%, the late majority 34% and laggards 16%. The bands come from a normal curve cut at one and two standard deviations from the mean.
  
  
    What is the Bass diffusion model?
    The Bass model (1969) forecasts adoption from two forces: innovation (p), adoption driven by outside influence such as advertising, and imitation (q), adoption driven by existing users. With market potential m, it predicts the size and timing of peak adoption.
  
  
    How do you use adopter categories in marketing?
    Match the argument to the group you are reaching. Early adopters respond to a clear advantage, the early majority needs proof and references, and the late majority needs low risk, a low price and evidence that most people already use it.

title: Importance-Performance Analysis Matrix

Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is importance-performance analysis?
    Importance-performance analysis (IPA) plots product or service attributes by how important customers say they are and how well the business performs on them. Martilla and James introduced it in 1977. The four quadrants show where to improve, what to protect and where effort may be wasted.
  
  
    What are the four quadrants of an IPA matrix?
    The four IPA quadrants are concentrate here (high importance, low performance), keep up the good work (high importance, high performance), low priority (low importance, low performance) and possible overkill (low importance, high performance).
  
  
    Where should the IPA cross-hairs go?
    Place IPA cross-hairs at the data means to compare attributes with each other and choose priorities. Place them at the scale midpoint to compare each attribute with a fixed standard. This tool offers both.
  
  
    What is the difference between IPA and SERVQUAL?
    SERVQUAL measures the gap between expected and perceived service on five set dimensions. IPA works with any attribute list and uses stated importance in place of expectations, which makes it quicker to run.

title: MMM Analyser
text:
In progress
Marketing mix modelling estimates how much each channel’s spend adds to sales, using the history of both. It captures two effects a simple regression misses: advertising keeps working after the week it runs, and each extra unit of spend adds less than the one before.
The model covers promotion spend and price. Product, place, people, process, and physical evidence are outside it, and are planned in the 7Ps Marketing Mix Planner.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. Spend and sales data never leave the browser. It opens on 2 years of weekly hotel booking revenue, generated from known settings, so you can see how closely the model recovers them.

title: MMM Analyser
text:
How it works
For each channel, spend is carried forward by an adstock rate, then passed through a saturation curve. Sales are modelled as a base, plus trend, seasonality, and price, plus the channel effects.
Adstock At = spendt + θ × At−1, with θ from 0 to 0.8Saturation h(A) = A ÷ (A + K), with K a multiple of the channel's mean adstockSalest = b0 + trend + seasonality + γ × pricet + Σ βc × hc(Ac,t)ROI = contribution ÷ spend. Marginal ROI = extra sales from one more unit of spend at the current level
For fixed θ and K the model is linear and is fitted by ordinary least squares. θ and K are chosen per channel by a search that maximises R². The tool warns when the data are too short for the number of coefficients, when a channel’s effect is negative and when two channels’ spend moves together so closely that their effects cannot be separated. Treat results as a starting point for testing budget shifts.

title: MMM Analyser
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is marketing mix modelling?
    Marketing mix modelling (MMM) is a statistical method that estimates how much each marketing channel's spend adds to sales, using the history of both. It captures carryover, where advertising keeps working after it runs, and diminishing returns.
  
  
    What is adstock in marketing mix modelling?
    Adstock is the carried-over effect of past advertising. With a carryover rate of 0.6, 60% of last week's effect carries into this week, then 60% of that into the next week.
  
  
    What is marginal ROI in marketing mix modelling?
    Marginal ROI is the extra sales from one more unit of spend at the current level. A channel with a high average ROI can have a low marginal ROI near saturation, which is the point to move budget elsewhere.
  
  
    How much data does marketing mix modelling need?
    Marketing mix modelling needs at least 10 periods for every coefficient. With four channels, trend, seasonality and price, that is about 90 periods or roughly 2 years of weekly data.

title: Product Life Cycle Stage Identifier
text:
In progress
Products tend to pass through four stages: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline. Each stage calls for a different marketing mix. This tool reads the stage from the shape of the sales history, and plots where the product sits on the curve.
Everything above runs in your browser and saves to this device only. It opens on quarterly bookings for a serviced apartment brand. Paste your own sales history, oldest period first.

title: Product Life Cycle Stage Identifier
text:
How it works
The tool fits a logistic curve, the classic S shape, to sales per period.
S(t) = K ÷ (1 + e−r(t − t0))K is the ceiling, r the growth rate, t0 the midpoint
The curve is fitted by searching over r and t0, with K solved by least squares at each step. Introduction runs until the curve reaches 10% of its ceiling, growth until 80% and maturity after that. A logistic curve never turns down, so decline is read from the data: two periods in a row falling by more than 5%.

title: Product Life Cycle Stage Identifier
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is the product life cycle?
    The product life cycle describes four stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Sales rise slowly, then quickly, then level off and eventually fall, and each stage calls for a different marketing mix.
  
  
    How do you identify the product life cycle stage?
    Read the stage from the shape of sales over time. This tool fits an S-curve to sales per period and places the latest period on it. Decline is detected when sales fall more than 5% in two periods in a row.
  
  
    What marketing mix suits each product life cycle stage?
    Introduction builds awareness and trial. Growth widens distribution and builds preference. Maturity defends share and differentiates. Decline prunes the range and cuts cost. The tool lists product, price, place and promotion priorities for the estimated stage.
  
  
    How much sales data does the product life cycle tool need?
    It needs at least 6 periods of equal length, such as quarters, and 12 or more gives a steadier fit. Seasonal sales work better once the seasonal pattern is removed.

title: RFM Segmentation Tool
text:
In progress
RFM segmentation groups customers by three facts about their buying: how recently they bought, how often and how much they spent. Those three facts predict who will buy again better than most demographic profiles, and they come straight from sales records.
Everything above runs in your browser. Transactions you paste stay on your device. The tool opens on 2 years of sample hotel bookings for 420 guests.

title: RFM Segmentation Tool
text:
How it works
Each customer gets a score from 1 to 5 on each measure, by quintile: the top fifth of customers scores 5 and the bottom fifth scores 1. Recency is reversed, so the most recent buyers score 5. Customers with tied values share a score.
Recency = days from the last purchase to the analysis dateFrequency = number of purchasesMonetary = total spendScore = 1 + the number of fifths of customers with a lower value
Segments come from the recency and frequency scores. Champions score 4 or 5 on both. At risk customers bought often, then went quiet. Lost customers score low on both. The monetary score separates the most valuable lapsed customers, labelled can’t lose them.

title: RFM Segmentation Tool
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is RFM analysis?
    RFM analysis is a customer segmentation method that scores each customer on recency (how recently they bought), frequency (how often they buy) and monetary value (how much they spend). Together the three scores predict who is likely to buy again.
  
  
    How do you calculate RFM scores?
    Rank customers on each measure and split them into fifths. The top fifth scores 5 and the bottom fifth scores 1, with recency reversed so the most recent buyers score 5. Customers with tied values share a score.
  
  
    What are the RFM customer segments?
    Common RFM segments are champions, loyal customers, potential loyalists, new customers, need attention, at risk, can't lose them, hibernating and lost. Each comes from a pattern of recency and frequency scores, and each suits a different campaign.
  
  
    What data do I need for RFM segmentation?
    RFM segmentation needs one row per transaction with a customer ID, a date and an amount. An export from a booking system, online shop or CRM usually has all three.

    What is STP marketing?
    STP marketing stands for segmentation, targeting and positioning. Segmentation divides a market into groups with similar needs, targeting chooses which group to serve and positioning designs the claim that group will hear.
  
  
    What makes a good market segment?
    A good market segment is measurable, large enough to be worth serving, reachable through channels you can use and different enough in its needs to justify its own offer.
  
  
    How do you write a positioning statement?
    A positioning statement names the target segment, the frame of reference, the point of difference and the evidence: for [segment] considering [frame], this is the option that [point of difference], evidenced by [proof].
  
  
    What comes after STP?
    The marketing mix comes after STP. This tool saves the positioning on your device, and the 7Ps Marketing Mix Planner and the Campaign Brief Generator read it from there.
  
  
    Is this STP Builder free?
    Yes. The STP Builder is free and opens straight away in any modern browser, including on a phone. Everything you enter is processed in your browser and stays on your device.

title: SWOT Analysis Builder
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is a SWOT analysis?
    A SWOT analysis is a planning framework that lists an organisation's strengths and weaknesses, which are internal and the opportunities and threats in its market, which are external. It gives a one-page view of where the organisation stands before a strategic decision.
  
  
    How do you prioritise a SWOT analysis?
    Score each item for impact and likelihood from 1 to 5 and multiply the two. The result, from 1 to 25, ranks every item across all four boxes, so the few items that need action stand apart from the many that only need watching.
  
  
    What is the difference between SWOT and PESTEL?
    PESTEL scans only the external environment: political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal forces. SWOT combines that outside view with an inside view of the organisation. A PESTEL is often the source of a SWOT's opportunities and threats.
  
  
    What is an example of a SWOT analysis for a hotel?
    A city hotel might list a direct website with all-in prices as a strength, dependence on booking platforms as a weakness, remote workers extending business trips as an opportunity, and rising platform commission as a threat. The demo on this page builds that example.

The Value Proposition Canvas, from Osterwalder and colleagues, sets what a business offers beside what a customer needs. The customer profile, the circle, lists the jobs the customer is trying to get done, the pains that get in the way, and the gains they hope for. The value map, the square, lists the products and services, the pain relievers and the gain creators. Fit means the square answers the circle.

title: Value Proposition Canvas
text:
How it works
Every pain and gain can be matched to one or more pain relievers or gain creators. Matches draw as dashed lines across the canvas.
Fit = pains and gains matched to at least one reliever or creator ÷ all pains and gains
A low fit score points to customer needs the offer leaves unanswered. A reliever or creator with no match points to features that answer no stated need.

Frequently Asked Questions

  
    What is the Value Proposition Canvas?
    The Value Proposition Canvas is a tool from Osterwalder and colleagues that matches what a business offers with what a customer needs. The customer profile lists jobs, pains and gains. The value map lists products and services, pain relievers and gain creators.
  
  
    How do you fill in a Value Proposition Canvas?
    Start with the customer profile, drawn from research: the jobs customers are trying to get done, their pains and the gains they want. Then design the value map to relieve the most important pains and create the most important gains.
  
  
    What is fit in the Value Proposition Canvas?
    Fit is reached when the value map answers the customer profile. This tool measures it as the share of pains and gains matched to at least one pain reliever or gain creator.
  
  
    How does the Value Proposition Canvas relate to the Business Model Canvas?
    It zooms in on two blocks of the Business Model Canvas: customer segments, which become the customer profile and value propositions, which become the value map.
